body.text: The Australian share market is likely to rise modestly on opening this morning, with ASX 200 futures up 15 points overnight.
Tech giant Google and its owner, Alphabet, lost more than half a trillion US dollars amid worries AI would subsume its advertising business, the largest one-day fall in the company's history.
See how the trading day unfolds on our blog.

Alphabet shares drop double digits
It's not often you see a 12% DROP on shares like Alphabet, but tank they did today.
It comes after the Google parent-company reported disappointing results in search advertising and a massive acceleration in cash burn as it poured resources into building out AI.
"In a market worried about AI cannibalizing the franchise, investors need to see search accelerating, not decelerating," said Dave Wagner, portfolio manager at Aptus Capital Advisors.
An area of success was Google Cloud - revenues more than doubled.

It's cash flow was car crash territory, more than $9b in the red - analysts had expected it to break even. It was spending big to boost cloud capacity and develop its AI Gemini, almost $6b last quarter. Reuters reports this is the first time it went into the negative in 22 years as a public company.

The Australian share market is making modest gains at the open of trade.
At 10:10am the ASX 200 was up 0.3% to 8,924.
Consumer cyclicals and healthcare are doing the heavy lifting.
Parliamentary inquiry into Australia Post welcomed
The union representing postal workers has welcomed a parliamentary inquiry into the future of Australia Post as a "positive step".

Communication Workers Union (CWU) National Secretary Shane Murphy said ensuring Australia Post is set up to deliver an accessible, affordable and reliable postal service for decades to come was crucial.
“There’s no question that when it comes to postal services, demand has changed. Australia Post needs to change with it, but that change needs to strengthen the service, not diminish it," he said.

“Uniform pricing and service obligations underpin the integrated network that ensures Australians can participate equally in the national economy, regardless of where they live or operate a business from."
ASX to open modestly higher
ASX Futures (SPI 200) is up 0.3%.
It's pointing to a modestly higher open of trade.
The 'fresh wave of anxiety' over AI
Gavin Friend Senior Markets Strategist NAB says a"fresh wave of anxiety over AI" has followed disappointing third-quarter earnings from Google parent company Alphabet.
Q3 earning news from Alphabet revealed disappointing search and advertising sales,
The results sent tech shares down with the tech-heave Nasdaq down 1.5 per cent and helping fuel a further push into the safety of bonds.
"Yields fell despite stronger US economic data in the form of Q3 GDP growth and an as-expected rise in core PCE inflation," Gavin Friend said.
The markets strategist said the Alphabet results underscored worries over AI and whether huge capital investment can generate returns quickly enough to justify valuations.

"While Microsoft earnings were better received, thanks to a surge in its cloud business, with capital expenditure remaining in check, Caterpillar’s modest earnings beat could not prevent a share slide," he wrote in an economic note.
Caterpillar has been significant in data centre buildout.
Govt launches inquiry into Australia Post
The Albanese government is launching a parliamentary inquiry in a bid to sure up the long-term viability of Australia Post.
The 217-year-old institution has faced challenges in recent times, with falling foot traffic at some post offices and a drop in letters.
Last financial year, there were about 1.42 billion letters sent through Australia Post — but that was down 14.7 per cent from the year before.
Communications Minister Anika Wells says changing consumer behaviour and commercial conditions posed significant challenges to the sustainability of Australia Post.
"That's why I've asked the House committee to explore how we can better support a sustainable and accessible postal service that delivers for all Australians," she said.
An Australia Post spokesperson said it looked forward to engaging constructively in the inquiry.

"For several years, we have highlighted the growing challenges facing Australia Post, which are shared by postal organisations around the world," they said."We welcome the government's action to address these challenges and support our long-term sustainability."

The inquiry is due to report back by the middle of next year.

Oil price still a thorn in the side of central banks
The price of Brent crude remains well above $100 a barrel.
Its price stayed elevated after an eventful night on Wall Street.
Here's an excerpt from investment firm MooMoo's morning note.

Wall Street turned decidedly sour as investors penalised tech heavyweights for aggressive spending and elusive pay-offs. Google parent Alphabet suffered its steepest single-day decline in company history, tumbling 12.6% as advertising revenue growth missed for the second consecutive, free cash flow was again negative, and a projected capital expenditure bill of up to US$205 billion raised sharp questions about profitability. The sell-off quickly spilled across enterprise software and cybersecurity, with ServiceNow cratering 27% and Fortinet sliding 20%.

Solid US economic growth of 3.4%, beating expectations of 3.2%, and an elevated 3.6% annual PCE inflation read reinforce that the US economy needs higher interest rates. While the tech sell-off dragged the US 10-year yield down to 4.94%, Brent crude remains above US$115 a barrel. These high financing costs leave companies with little room for operational slips. Local investors should watch whether market breadth continues to narrow, testing if high-yielding sectors can hold the line.
'Nasty week for global markets'
Capital.com senior financial market analyst Kyle Rodda has given a sobering assessment of the week that was on financial markets.
"It's turning into a nasty week for global markets, as the slew of event risk that market participants have been forced to tackle yields greater rather than less uncertainty," he notes this morning.

"Tech results have turned into a tale of woe, with Alphabet's historic plunge following its highly underwhelming results emulated by Amazon after it published its quarterly earnings after the closing bell.
"Meanwhile, central bankers, while hardly rattling the proverbial cage, continue to guide the markets towards future rate hikes.

"On top of that, energy markets are pricing in an escalation in the US and Iran war that's feared will come after US midterms. The midterm elections, as they are wont to do, are stifling market sentiment too."

Key Event
Amazon hit in after-hours trade after disappointing results
The tech pain looks set to bleed into tomorrow's US session, after a negative initial reception to Amazon's third quarter results.
The company reported earnings per share of $US1.89, which missed typical analyst forecasts of $US1.97, despite strong performance in its Amazon Web Services cloud computing business.
Its capital expenditure of $US77.3 billion massively exceeded analyst expectations of $US58.67 billion, leading to negative trailing free cash flow of $US42.4 billion over the past year.
The company's shares were down around 6% in after-hours trade according to Bloomberg.

Westpac economist Ryan Wells said oil prices remained elevated overnight amid ongoing geopolitical uncertainty
Brent Crude rose 0.6 per cent to US$116/bbl as reports that US President Donald Trump was being briefed on military options for Iran renewed concerns over a potential escalation.
Local equities to 'sidestep' Wall St tech sell-off
Moo Moo's chief market strategist Tapas Strickland said he's expecting a "much more subdued open" than what is indicated by ASX 200 futures, is likely this morning.
This is given sharp falls in post-market trade by Amazon (-6%) and Intel (-20%).
Overnight, the US technology sector sold off sharply with the Nasdaq Composite down 1.4% and S&P 500 falling 0.3%.
Major commodities also fell in sympathy – copper down 1.1% and gold dipping 0.4% – which will weigh on Australian miners.
"Wall Street turned decidedly sour as investors penalised tech heavyweights for aggressive spending and elusive pay-offs," he said.
He said even Microsoft dipped despite delivering 19% revenue growth, "burdened by plans" to issue US$25 billion in debt to fund infrastructure.

Key Event
ECB joins the October interest rate hold club

We've had a flurry of central bank meetings this week, with the Bank of Canada lifting its benchmark rate for the first time in three years to 2.5%, while the Reserve Bank of New Zealand surprised markets by staying on hold at 2.75% and the US Fed surprised no-one by doing the same to keep rates at 3.75-4%.
Last night it was the turn of the European Central Bank, which stuck with the on-hold club.
"The ECB kept its policy rates unchanged at its October meeting and reiterated a data-dependent, meeting-by-meeting approach to setting policy," writes ANZ's G3 economist Brian Martin.
"We continue to think that the ECB will raise the deposit facility rate 25bp [basis points] to 2.75% at its next meeting in December.

"The dovish signal in the post-meeting statement that tighter financial conditions, owing to the rise in government bond yields, will weigh on growth and inflation, was offset by President Lagarde retaining a hawkish bias and noting that the Governing Council had considered a rate hike at this meeting. Market expectations for further hikes were ultimately little changed on the day.
"Lagarde announced she will depart the ECB in February. Pablo Hernandez de Cos and Klaas Knot are the frontrunners to replace her."
Next cab off the rank is the Bank of Japan later today, with markets pricing just a 2% chance it will hike today, but an 80% chance it will raise rates in December.
Of course, the Reserve Bank of Australia meets next Monday and Tuesday, with markets this morning pricing around a 90% chance of a rate hike being announced at 2:30pm AEDT on November 3.

I had a great chat with Carrington yesterday about the various central bank decisions to that point, of which the most interesting was the RBNZ's hold against 95% market expectations it would raise rates.
Investors becoming more discerning about how AI growth is funded, warns analyst

There's an interesting dichotomy between Google parent company Alphabet's third quarter results and their disastrous reception — a 12.6%, roughly $US500 billion share value wipe-out — and rival Microsoft.
Microsoft's share price barely moved overnight, off just 0.2% to $US530.14.

Betashares investment strategist Hugh Lam said the divergence reflects concern that Alphabet's free cash flow remained negative for a second consecutive quarter, while Microsoft is still able to fund its AI expansion while retaining positive free cash flow.
"The market is moving from indiscriminately rewarding AI spending to scrutinising how it is financed," he writes.

"The sell-off came despite clear green shoots at Alphabet. Google Cloud revenue rose 103% year-on-year to $30.7 billion, and the division's operating margin expanded to 36.2% from 23.7% a year earlier. Usage is growing too, with the Gemini app reaching one billion users.
"The key question is whether Alphabet's 2027 capex, which management expects to increase significantly, converts into Cloud revenue fast enough to bring free cash flow back into positive territory."
Key Event
Alphabet sheds half a trillion US dollars in worst fall on record as AI cracks widen
Investors appear to be becoming increasingly nervous about the artificial intelligence rollout, particularly following Alphabet results that disappointed the market.
Investors were spooked by the Google parent company's increased cash burn as its investment in AI exceeded its current ability to generate profits.
The company's Google Services unit missed quarterly revenue expectations by just over $US2 billion, generating $US96.3 billion, as growth in search revenue slowed.
Reuters reports that Alphabet's negative free cash flow of $US9.1 billion shocked analysts, who had generally expected it to come close to breaking even.
Alphabet told investors it plans to further increase its investment spending from this year's forecasts of around $US200 billion.
That saw its shares record their worst fall since listing, plunging 12.6% to $US283.82, wiping close to $US500 billion off its market valuation in one day.
That was enough to drive the Nasdaq down 1.4%, compared to modest 0.3% falls for the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average.
